Well, Dial a Teacher is a program that the City Council has funded for years and it is a program where we have seven different languages now. Uh, where students call in and get homework. It’s a homework help hotline basically. But you’re doing it with a teacher. Uh, and you know we’ve expanded it. We do a lot of it - it is an online service now but because the students felt more comfortable with it as students develop new ways of learning and doing their work, you have to modernize to it. Yes, because there’s a lot of - especially if there’s not an afterschool program, there are a lot of students who don’t have anyone to help them with their homework and that’s a difficult thing to do in life, especially if you’re having a hard time. I don’t want to go into math. I know nobody likes new math. Nobody has liked new math for 40 years. Whatever the new math is, nobody likes it, okay but you know you don’t have to worry about that. We have people who know whatever the new math is.

Uh, so we’ll take care of that but yes, it is something and it’s constantly utilized.
And the funding is only 300, around 300K.
That’s it.
How many students actually, you got the help in this program?
There’s 83,000 last year.
83,000 so it’s much cheaper to invest in this type of program right?
Yeah, yeah.
Cheaper than like a consultant right? If we can -
Cheaper than consultants.
We could hire one consultant to give me leadership development.
And the help, you said 18,000 students right?
80,000 students. So, how many students you can hire?
Which, according to new math, 80 is greater than 18.
Yeah, 80 and then one million dollar, how much - you can imagine how many kids we can help. Thank you.
Yeah, thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Joseph.
Three rapid questions for you. Oh yeah, Mayoral control, yes or no for the next four years?
No.
Teacher Centers?
Yes.
And Childcare Navigators?

Childcare Navigator is, I’m sorry, childcare navigator is - that was developed between ourselves and two companies and one company was dealing with the financial side in terms of what a family might qualify for for assistance from a city, state, or federal government in terms of childcare. Uh, as well as what the costs are at the actual centers themselves. Uhm and the other company was where everything is. So, one was dealing with the paperwork and then the other was where the locations are, what type of

students they serve. That’s all together now in what is known as the Childcare Navigator. So, you could put in your zip code and say put in the different parameters you want. It will take you about five minutes and you would then know exactly what your options were for childcare for you and your child. This is something we put together. I do believe, I’m - I do believe that the city has an RFP out for a $100,000 million contract to develop and navigate it, which they already have access to. So, the navigator is to me, we developed it because we thought it would be the pivotal tool to actually help families. It only came out of frustrations because our own members were constantly struggling looking for childcare that was appropriate for them or affordable to them as well as the different parents in all the communities who work inside the city were constantly frustrated by it and that’s why we went and pushed towards that.
Does it also cater to zero to two or -
Hmm, hmm.
Okay.
Yup.
Thank you Chair.
Thank you Council Member. I want to thank -
Mayoral control.
On your rapid fire questions.
Rapid fire two, mayoral control.
Uh, I’ll take that one, the other one is more UFT uh, I would say uhm, no to four years. I think that uh we haven’t heard enough about what the vision for the education of our city is yet.
Okay.

From the Mayor and the Chancellor. Uh, I don’t have a personal grievance of any sort but again, every, every school in the City of New York and in the state, is required the principal with their chapter leader to develop a plan for their school.
Hmm, hmm and what about a safety plan?
And then I’m sorry -
Go ahead.
Former Chair. Then we align the school's budget to that plan.
Okay.

But a 40 plus billion dollar bureaucracy can’t tell us a plan for the future and how they want to align that budget and make it transparent. So, I think if it’s good for the geese, good for the gander.
Okay.
What’s the plan?
What’s the plan?
What’s the plan?
That’s the hundred million dollar question.
Too often, we -
$40 billion.
$40 billion.
Too often has the initiatives but not necessarily a strategic plan.
Okay.
And before we hand someone a license for four years, I think we should have more information on it, so let’s try two and see how it goes.
Okay.

Thank you Council Member and as you know, we had our hearing on Mayoral Control and a number of the things that were mentioned here was brought up there, including is there a comprehensive educational plan for the city instead of just initiatives? Including issues about contracting, oversight of contracts, so we can really get into making sure our money is going to the kids and two methods that we know work, not necessarily consultants. But I want to thank both of you for the work you do for our city every day.
Thank you.
For the work on behalf of your members and for the work that you’re doing really in collaboration, which is really incredible to see. Thank you so much.
What an outstanding hearing. Thank you.
Thank you. I’d like to now call Donald Nesbit, Vice President of Local 372 of DC 37.

Good afternoon Chair, Chair Dinowitz, and distinguished members of the Council.

I am Donald Nesbit, Executive President for Local 372 DC 37 AFSCME. We represent 24,000 members and schools, 8,000 plus School Lunch Workers. Our members, as School Lunch Workers, serve 946,747 public school children and get them ready for learning. School Lunch Workers unload, prepare, and serve food each day, including during the summer months. School lunch is critical in a student's health and well-being, it also ensures that students have the nutrition that is needed throughout the day. It is important that there is sufficient kitchen staff to service these menus. Local 372 respectfully requests that the city allocate $10 million towards hiring of 1,000 School Lunch Workers, bringing the total number in service up to 9,000 plus. This will help reduce the strain on the current workforce while still continuing to fulfill the breakfast and lunch initiatives set by previous administrations. School Lunch Workers must also accommodate dietary restrictions, including medical or religious restrictions. School food programs accommodate such restrictions, School food workers must follow

multiple sets of strict guidelines to ensure school for children are eating safely. Breakfast in the Classroom is one of those programs we prepare - we prepare for and also prepare for lunch. Local 372 is extremely supportive of these programs, as well as universal lunch – every child deserves to come to class with a full stomach. So, an additional 1,000 school lunch workers, it would make it uh - is essential, so it’s not as difficult on the current workforce. Another struggle faced by school lunch employees is updating the existing inadequate cooling and air exchange within our kitchens. That has become a struggle for decades to school lunch workers. The majority of schools built from the 1930 and 1990, lack the proper design and operation for adequate indoor air circulation. A 2017 report titled “Too Hot to Learn,” detailed the significant lack of air conditioning where the mayor and elected officials pushed for support for air conditioning in teaching spaces, which was essential. That same energy and leadership is needed to support the health and safety of thousands of School Lunch Workers.

We thank former Council Members Treyger and other members of the Council at the time in pushing for uhm, for Resolutions to this. Local 372 requests that the DOE and the SCA come out with a comprehensive plan to evaluate the school outstanding kitchen ventilation needs throughout the five boroughs, and we request more funding be allocated towards a plan pursuant to this evaluation. Again, we extend our gratitude to the Council. We hope that we have your support in the request for $10 million for more staff within the school kitchens and also, additional resources to remediate these working conditions. Thank you.
Thank you Vice President Nesbit. Do you have an approximate vacancy rate of current budgeted headcount?

Uh, we’re short - so school food has uhm - I want to thank the Council for this two years ago. We came here asking for $20 million. Chair Rita at the time, Rita JOseph, pushed for along with the Council Members, for this funding. This funding went into not only education around nutrition within schools. But it also went towards staffing, which was critical but what we’re finding as a

trustee at the retirement system as well, the headcount that we get in, folks are retiring and leaving at the same rate. And so, it’s just filling the gaps but we’re still short and we think about a thousand more workers will be adequate in order to fill these gaps permanently.
And can you speak to some of the struggles with hiring and recruiting uh, new - uh new employees.

So, one is uh my colleagues within labor spoke before at the Principals Union and others President Mulgrew has spoken to. Retention and recruitment is the same across the board for city workers. In an affordability crisis where things continue to go up, we have to figure out a way to raise wages for workers. Starting salaries is a big stopping point for a lot of folks. Uhm, and so, that’s the main issue in how much folks are getting paid. If you are taking a job and still can’t afford to pay your rent right? And still have to take a second or third job in order to live, that just doesn’t work at some point.

Right and then I mean how many employed people are also living in shelters for that very same reason who are in unions right? So, we hear time and again, uhm, as you mentioned whether it’s serving food, early childhood education, school safety, wages need to go up. Uhm, do you have an estimate about how many lunchrooms or what investment would need to be made to ensure that the workers are safe and air conditioned even in the old buildings, what kind of investment that would require?

So, the estimates I think two years ago were about $70 million uhm in order to take care of this project. I will say uhm I’m grateful to the school leadership. Some of the money that they’ve had in their own budget, Chris and his team have actually put money into a list of outstanding projects in ventilation systems that they needed to upgrade within kitchens. So, uhm, according to that list, he’s put in some of his own money so I would guess that it’s not the same amount as it was two years ago but there’s still a great need. And we work, just so you know we work closely with Chris and team and labor management for them to make sure that we’re getting up to date information and our team and

reps are also out in the fields to ensure that we’re looking at these uhm conditions and that we’re reporting back uh where there are needs.
Okay, thank you so much Mr. Vice President.
Thank you Chair. Thank you Council Member.

Uhm, we’re now going to continue the public testimony portion of the hearing. I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today’s topic, the

Preliminary Education and School Construction Authority Budget. We will hear all in person testimony first and then turn to testimony on Zoom. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. I will now call the next panel. And if at any point I mispronounce your name, I apologize, you’ll correct me for the record. Uhm, Angela Hernandez, Connie Chen, Adrina Rokib, Mariama Jalloh, Anyinelda Santana Candelier, Paulina Milewska, and Ammy Heredia. You may approach the dais. We will begin this panel. We’ll start from my right, your left. You’ll state your name for the record, begin your testimony and remember you have two minutes to testify. You may begin when you’re ready.

Hello, my name is Angela Hernandez and I attend the Young Women's Leadership School in the Bronx and I’m a youth activist with the Ya-Ya Network. Today I stand before you all because as a student from a low income Black and brown

school, I would love to see the city’s budget actively prioritizing the youths mental wellbeing. Within my school, a frequent problem is conflicts between students. After a fight breaks out between two students, the two are suspended for about a week or two. However, when they return back to the school, not only are they behind on their school work but the tension between the two will remain with some cases being that another fight will occur. Although there is a restorative justice club within our school, many have not even heard of its existence, including myself, however, I know that the club could be doing so much more for the community but the limited budget has held it from its full potential. That’s why I’m asking the City Council to invest $80 million to expand mental health and restorative justice practices within New York City and its schools in order to create a safe space for its students. We can fund this cause not by filling the open positions for school safety agents, which students have frequently stated that who cause distress and unsafety for many of the students here. Thank you for listening.
Thank you so much. They’ll reset - you can begin when ready. They will reset your time. You worry about you. Just go ahead whenever you’re ready.

Alright, good afternoon to the Education Committee. My name is Connie Chen and I speak to you today as an immigrant student attending Stuyvesant High School. Some students around me are worrying about their next math test, college applications or they work in clubs. Immigrant students are worried if their family will be here tomorrow. We have additional responsibilities that our peers never have to stress about. From translating important documents to being a parental figure to our siblings. Even with these burdens, immigrant students go through our school system every single day. I remember when a student from my school jokingly called ICE on one of his friends. Despite it being a joke, his friend was terrified that ICE would come and take him or his parents. The fact that students even feel comfortable joking about this should tell you that schools are not adequately informing their students.

We should not fear that our schools might comply with ICE. Yet, we have every reason to be afraid. Dylan Lopez Contreras from ELLIS Preparatory Academy, [INAUDIBLE 41:38] from Gotham Collaborative High School. A six year old student from public school 89. All of these names are students that have been detained by ICE due to the failure of their schools and their city to protect them. Students already face enough stress. Don’t burden them knowing that at any second, they could be left without a family to go to. Imagine being a kid, and all you want is support from your parents. You open your front door and everything is exactly how it was when you left for school but your house feels empty. The laundry is still being dried, moms book is on her nightstand. Dad's coffee and book is still on the table but they’re not there and you don’t know if they’ll ever come back. That has been reality - sorry, that has been reality for so many students in New York City and we’re counting on you to make sure fear has no place in education. We want the city to fully fund protections, both immigrant students and their families. We want

baseline funding for the immigrant family communications and outreach, which expires in June. Thank you.
Thank you so much. Perfect timing. Please make sure your uhm, you could push the button on the base.

Good afternoon Council Members. My name is Adrina Rokib and I am here today on behalf of the Ya-Ya Network to speak about a basic dignity that too many students in our city are being denied. Imagine a student sitting in class when she suddenly gets her menstrual cycle. Maybe for the first time, she is confused, scared, and has no products. Can you imagine your own child facing that panic and if no product is available, the humiliation of leaking through her clothes in front of her classmates. Yet our schools are failing them. This panic is far too common. Students get their periods abruptly with no warning and no resources. The anxiety at that moment is a burden no child should carry. In 2016 New York City made history as the first city in the nation to require free menstrual products in schools but almost a decade later implementation remains a failure. A 2023 survey found that 85

percent of NYC High School students still lacked access. Just last year, a lawsuit was filed alleging the DOE is still in flagrant violation with students routinely missing class because they cannot access what they need. Even when products exist they are often behind a pay wall or are so low quality they don’t work. For students from low income families who make up over 70 percent of NYC public school students, an extra quarter for a pad or a tampon is an impossible choice. It is inconsiderate, it is inequitable and it is a healthcare issue. You have the power to change this. We need dedicated funding and accountability for reinforcing the past legislation that the city has failed to implement. Menstrual products are not luxuries. I would argue that they are essential as toilet paper. I urge you to make menstrual equity a reality for every student in New York City. My colleagues are here today demanding funds to support the services that make our schools safe and supportive communities, including funding for restorative justice and counselors, not cops. Dedicated funding for menstrual products is one more

way to increase students' sense of being safe and cared for. Thank you.
Thank you so much. Next.

Good afternoon. My name is Anyinelda Santana, I am 17 years old and a senior at Academy for Excellence and leadership. I am also a youth leader with Make the Road New York at the Bushwick Campus Student Success Center. In my role, I guide my peers through every step of their post secondary planning exploring options and applying to colleges and navigating financial aid. I also support them in the social emotional aspect of decision making, helping them stay focused, motivated and confident about their future. When I began high school, I wasn’t sure what path to take. I was torn between psychology and nursing but after completing my youth leader summer training and doing deeper research, I discovered my true passion, nursing. A career where I can make a direct impact on people's lives. Being a youth leader has shown me not just about how essential a student's success center is on campus. It provides students with personalized one-on-one support that helps them navigate high school and prepare for college with confidence.

Without it, many students will be left to figure out the complex process of FASPA and TAP on their own. Often missing out on opportunities that could change their future. My family’s story shows the difference a student's success center can make. My big sister who was part of the center was first in our immediate family to apply to college. She is now a first year nursing major at CUNY City Tech. Watching her support students and serve as a role model inspired me to step into the role and become a youth leader myself. Now, I can provide the same guidance and encouragement and inspiration my peers that I once received. This work not only taught me how to help others but also to grow, lead and unite my community towards their dream. The SSE has given me a family of peers and mentors who push me to strive for excellence every day. They remind me that with their support and determination, anything is possible. If funding for SSE is cut, thousands of students will lose access to guidance that truly changed the trajectory of their lives. We will need the city to commit to $3.3 million this year to sustain the Student Success

Center across the New York City. Supporting these centers -
Thank you so much. Thank you and remember you can submit the rest for testimony.
Thank you.

Thank you so much. Uhm, just if this panel could raise their hands, just raise your hand if it’s true. Have your teachers or administrators or adults in your school spoken to you like about ICE and what that means in your school and any guidance or support on the issue? So, what I’m seeing is for in none of your schools, Stuyvesant Young Women’s Leadership Academy, none of your teachers or administrators have spoken or given you guidance on ICE? Okay, and can you just talk briefly for 15 seconds on if it was impactful or not, what that looked like.
I feel like it was impacting because they taught us about our uhm, like the rights that we have uhm, so that like if ICE comes to your door, like what you can do.
Uhm, hmm, thank you.
So, I feel like it has.

Thank you. Thank you for sharing that. Uhm, I want to uhm, and raise your hand if you’ve had - if you’ve been taught restorative in your current school, restorative justice practices as part of your daily class or like in school activities. Okay, so clearly there’s in your particular schools, more that needs to be communicated about ICE, something that’s facing so many of our schools and our students and restorative justice, which we so deeply care about in this Council. Uhm, I want to thank the four of you for your advocacy, for your testimony. You know of course the work, the discussions we’ve had outside of this hearing. Thank you so much. I’m going to call the next panel but before I do, just if you do at any point need a translation, you’d like to testify and you need translation, please see the Sergeant up here. [SPEAKING IN SPANISH 420:00-420:08] Thank you. The next panel, Serenity DeJesus, Ashley Frato, Daniel Ruiz, Ny’Jhea Pulley, Ishaq Bekoe, Jiaxiang Zhang. I apologize, you’ll correct me please and Deniella Rodriguez. Thank you.

Okay, we can begin on my right, your left. Starting with you sir, please state your name for the record and you may begin your testimony. Whenever you’re ready sir.

Hello Education Committee Members. My name is Jiaxiang and I am a sophomore at Stuyvesant High School and a fellow with friends of the highline. I am in support of the Transit Authorities Alliance Expand Student OMNY Campaign because I believe we students should have universal access, a fair communication regarding deactivation and a better process for replacing lost or deactivated OMNY cards. Now, before I begin, I’d like to make it clear that some of the information that I’m providing is specific to Stuyvesant High School although there may be some common ground with the information. Having the OMNI cards are - is an important part of every student's commute to and from commitments, however, since the debut of OMNI cards, there have been a lot of issues with most of which is covered in today’s testimony. As a volunteer in my schools guidance office, I have seen first hand the amount of OMNI replacement

forms my schools transport coordinator receives daily due to lost cards or OMNI cards seizing the work. Most students who submitted an OMNI replacement form were due to the OMNI card not working. On December 4, 2025, exactly three months since the school year began, 528 OMNI replacement forms have been submitted with 284 of them being submitted due to OMNI cards seizing the work. Stuyvesant ran out of OMNI cards on March 2, 2026. This morning we received an order of 200 OMNI cards, three weeks after we had initially ran out. In the month of March received 185 OMNI replacement cards and counting. The agency system is supposed to trigger a new OMNI card delivery when a school's available OMNI card falls below 300. Since we received 200 today, does that mean we’ll receive another delivery? Based on previous experiences, most likely not. Additionally, ATS’s data on Stuyvesant High School is wildly inaccurate. And thus, I ask the Committee to expand student OMNI and work on more communication with all of our schools and to develop a system with accurate data.
Thank you Jiaxiang.

Good afternoon Chair and members of the Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Ishaq Bekoe and I am a student at NYC Lab School for Collaborative Studies. I am here today with the highlight and strong support of Transportation Alliances Expand Student OMNI Campaign. Transportation is not just about getting to and from school. It directly affects the students ability to fully participate in life. OMNI supports hundreds of thousands of New York City Public School Students who rely on public transport every single day. Expanding access to unlimited rides would allow students to move freely and safely throughout the city, not just for school but for jobs, internships, tutoring, extra curricular activities and even family responsibilities, like picking up younger siblings. Right now, limited rides create unnecessary barriers where students are forced to choose between opportunity simply because they cannot afford the extra fare. That should not be a reality in a city like New York. Transportation should not be a barrier. Last year, my friend's OMNI card randomly stopped working. We never knew why and to this day, we still

don’t know why. He tried to use it and it kept saying card not accepted. We thought it was just a glitch, however, the next day, the same thing happened. His card wasn’t working so he had to jump the turnstile where an officer approached him and stopped him and asked him where his OMNI card was. He tried to explain to the officer that his OMNI card wasn’t working, to which the officer replied that something like that doesn’t just happen. My friend ended up showing the officer his school idea then missed a train causing him to wait another ten minutes. When a student - when a student's card stops working without warning, it is not just an inconvenience, it can disrupt their entire day, their attendance and their sense of stability and this is one of many stories of cards mysteriously stopped, not working. That is why fair and transparent communication around deactivations is just as important as expanding access. Students deserve to know what is happening and how to resolve issues without confusion or delay. Every student in New York City deserves equal access of the opportunities this school has - I mean this city has to offer.

Expanding Student OMNI is not just a transportation policy, it is an investment in students' future. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Thank you so much. You may begin when ready. Make sure your microphone is on. The red light means it’s on. NY’JEAH

Good afternoon Committee Chair and members of the Committee. My name is Ny’Jhea Pulley and I am a sophomore at High School for the Environmental States. I’m here with the highline as part of the Friend of the Highline Fellows program. I’m very grateful and appreciative to have this opportunity to share my testimony with all of you. As two of the country's largest systems, MTA and New York City Public Schools serve millions of students each year. Without public transportation, the city can’t function, which is why I believe Student OMNI must expand. There are around 600,000 students who use the MTA regularly and are a part of the student OMNI card system. In theory, four passes should be more than enough for students but as a student athlete, who is also part of their extra curriculars, four passes just

isn’t enough. I often find myself calculating how much money I need to spend in order to get through a whole day even with four passes. I play school and club volleyball and that has been a big difficulty for me. I would use one pass to take the train to get to school, one pass to take the train to go to like around the area of my way game, then another pass to take the bus to the school, which I was playing at and then after the game, I would use one pass to go to my club practice and that was four passes. So, to get home, I would have to pay with my own money. In my case, I had fare money or if I didn’t, I would ask my mom but not every student has that privilege of being able to pay the price every time. In summary, every student deserves to do all their extra curricular activities and out of school responsibilities without having to pay out of pocket with students on the expansions this could be. Thank you for your time.
Thank you Ny’Jhea.

Good afternoon Committee Chair and Members of the Committee. My name is Daniel Ruiz, I am a 10th grade student in Quest to Learn and I’m

representing the friends of the highline. Before I begin with my testimony, I would like to thank the Committee for holding this hearing and my manager for allowing me to state my stance on such a subject. The MTA system is one that many New Yorkers rely on and students like my fellow coworkers and I use the system to get to school, go to extra curriculars or college programs or to spend times with friends or family. More student passes are beneficial but increasing that number can greatly help students across New York City to get to all their commitments and other responsibilities easily. Therefore, I advocate for unlimited rides and OMNI cards for students. As stated before, the OMNI cards for students are beneficial in a lot of ways. Off a bullet pointed list, some things the students use the cards are getting to and from school using transfer in between, using the MTA system during lunch to get food in a timely manner, getting to part time jobs which can also take multiple transfers, exploring places, whether it be finding a new park or finding a new store to spend their time in or hanging out with friends which could also be another subgroup for

exploring places. These benefits, as well as many others allow students to move freely throughout the city, providing educational and mental health benefits. From my experience, the OMNI card ride restrictions are a little detrimental to me. I enjoy hanging out with my friends usually after school, after work, or on weekends and sometimes my friends and I go around Manhattan and sometimes around Queens and the four rides OMNI are, most of the time, not enough for me. I also use my OMNI to meet with my mother to run errands before my job and having only four rides makes it going from Chelsea to South Jamaica harder. Thus, I ask the Committee to help fund unlimited rides, increasing student mobility across the city and overall providing an even more beneficial experience for students. Thank you.
That was great. Thank you so much Daniel.

My name is Serenity DeJesus. I am a 9th grader at the Community School for Social Justice. I am here to share my experience with the New York Edge Community Schools and tell you how New York Edge has strengthened our school for the better.

New York Edge is not just the afterschool program for our school. They are an engaging and enriching all day program that gives promising students like me, opportunities to improve our overall attendance, behavior and academics. For example, they launched an exciting initiative called New Year, New Me that awards students who improve and maintain their attendance with deli vouchers, uh, with vouchers to our local deli. The PBIS school store and book system reframes positive behavior, good attendance, and high grades. In a way, it also teaches us real world skills like personal accountability and financial literacy. New York Edge has brought in an inclusive and interactive way of approaching our history and culture. As an example, our Black history month event, featured a cuisine focused activity where we use our literacy and finan- and uh investigation skills to research Black owned restaurants and recipes. New York Edge has this - The New York Edge staff has the sort of presence that will put a smile on my face, even on my worst of days. Every morning, when I come into school, I will always be greeted with a good morning and a smile. I

went from coming to school once a week to every day. The New York Edge team has motivated me to show up to school more consistently, become more involved in school activities and embrace positivity all the way. Please vote to increase funding to New York Edge in the upcoming city budget. Investing in New York Edge means investing in students like me. Thank you.

That was great and I got say real profits like every school student keeping it at like two minutes. I could tell you wrote this, you practiced, it’s very clear. Just kudos to all of you. There it is, you got 12 seconds to spare. You did fantastic. You’ve all been doing - thank you so much and by the way, I know it takes a lot for students just to be in school all day. Like your school work is a lot and for you to come here and also testify on behalf of you- not just yourself but your community is really an incredible thing to see. So, simply for coming here and doing your school work and taking care of your siblings and all the preparation you did for this, uh, you’re really making your New York City, your classmates proud. You’re really showing what our city really is and it’s about all of you so thank you for testifying.

Next, please.

Good afternoon. My name is Ashley Frato, I’m the New York Edge Community School director at the community school for social justice. I’m here today to ask that you prioritize New York Edges Fiscal Year ‘27 citywide funding requests. New York Edge is the city’s oldest and largest provider of after school summer programming, serving almost 33,000 students in 134 schools across the city, including 4 beacon centers and 21 community schools. We run programs in 37 of the 51 Council Districts. Our mission is to help bridge the opportunity gap among students in under invested communities. Core components of our programming include stem education, social, emotional learning and leadership, visual and performing arts, sports, health and wellness, academics and college and career readiness and summer programs. We are as identified by Mosaic by ACT, the largest after school provider in the nation offering social and emotional learning supports. This year, we are seeking $1.5 million under the Council’s After School Enrichment initiative and $250,000 under the Council’s Social and Emotional Supports for Students

initiative. For over three decades, the New York City Council has been a vital partner in helping us to fulfill our mission.
